problem.title: Card-fraud scoring service
problem.context: A payments company scores every card transaction for fraud before it is authorized. It processes about 3,000 transactions per second on a normal day and up to five times as many during seasonal sales. Fraudsters adapt within weeks, and the confirmed fraud labels (chargebacks) arrive days to weeks after the transaction. Auditors and the card schemes can ask, months later, why a given transaction was scored the way it was. The ML team has five data scientists and two ML engineers. The company's operations team runs the data centres and the shared infrastructure, but there is no platform team for machine learning.

requirements.text: Score every card transaction before the authorization decision, using the cardholder's recent activity (for example, the spending of the last hour and the last day).
Update the model as new confirmed fraud cases arrive.
For any past score, show which model version and which input values produced it.
During a seasonal peak of 15,000 transactions per second, a score comes back within 30 ms at the 99th percentile.
When the scoring service or one of its data sources fails, authorizations go on. The business accepts weaker fraud detection for up to 15 minutes, but no authorization may fail because of scoring.
An auditor asks about a score from up to 13 months ago. Within one working day the team answers with the model version, the input values and the training data that model was built from.
When the fraud loss rate rises in one segment, a retrained model can be in production within 48 hours, after it has been compared with the current model on recent transactions.
Card data must stay inside the company's PCI-certified environment: no external service may process it.
Seven people build and run the system, with no dedicated ML platform team.

trajectory.hypothesis: Together these decisions address online scoring, reliability, audit and model adaptation within the company's environment and team constraints.
trajectory.observation: The design explicitly supplies recent features, a failure fallback, historical score and training records, and monitored retraining. The text does not provide benchmark evidence for the latency target, a strict 48-hour promotion bound, or operating-cost evidence for the small team.

values: Ingestion: Kafka transaction topic
Feature state: Flink aggregates in Redis
Serving: Python REST container on Kubernetes
Capacity: Six replicas with CPU autoscaling
trajectory.hypothesis: R1 and Q1 favor precomputed recent activity and horizontally scalable online scoring; C1 keeps the path inside the certified environment.
trajectory.observation: Maintained aggregates avoid rebuilding recent activity per request, and replicas can spread peak load. The selected technologies do not by themselves prove the 30 ms p99 or low operating burden.

values: Feature state: Query historical transaction tables for each score
trajectory.hypothesis: Check whether Q1 forces maintained per-card feature state instead of computing recent aggregates from historical data on each request.
trajectory.observation: A per-request historical query can represent recent activity, but adds work to the synchronous scoring path and weakens the latency case at peak. The available requirements favor maintained state, though they do not uniquely require Flink and Redis.

values: Authorization behavior: Synchronous call with rule-engine fallback
trajectory.hypothesis: Q2 requires authorization to continue on scoring failure; R1 still calls for a score in the normal path.
trajectory.observation: A bounded synchronous call preserves use of the model for ordinary transactions, while the existing rule engine ensures a failed score does not fail authorization.

values: Score record: Append-only on-premises object-store table for 13 months
Experiment lineage: MLflow records parameters, metrics, training snapshot and artifact
trajectory.hypothesis: R3 and Q3 call for preserved score inputs and model identity, plus recoverable training provenance; C1 requires local handling of card data.
trajectory.observation: The score log captures model version and inputs for the full audit horizon, and MLflow links model artifacts to a training data snapshot. Together these support reconstruction of the score and training set.

values: Score record: Keep only the latest score and model version
trajectory.hypothesis: Check whether R3 and Q3 force retained per-score history rather than keeping only the latest score metadata.
trajectory.observation: Overwriting score history loses the inputs and model identity for older decisions, so the audit requirements force a retained historical record. The exact object-store implementation remains a free choice among suitable durable stores.

values: Retraining: Nightly Airflow pipeline on last 90 days of labels
Experiment lineage: MLflow records parameters, metrics, training snapshot and artifact
Promotion: Three-day shadow comparison and manual risk-team promotion
trajectory.hypothesis: R2 and Q4 call for repeated retraining on newly available labels, comparison with current production behavior, and a governed promotion path.
trajectory.observation: Nightly retraining reacts to delayed confirmed labels, and shadow evaluation satisfies the comparison intent. Three days of shadowing plus manual action can exceed the 48-hour production bound, so the workflow only partly meets Q4. MLflow and Airflow are plausible tools for this team but the team-size constraint does not force them.

values: Promotion: Promote every nightly model automatically without comparison
trajectory.hypothesis: Check whether Q4's required comparison makes comparison-free automatic promotion an unacceptable alternative.
trajectory.observation: Skipping comparison loses an explicit Q4 requirement and can put an unchecked model into production. Comparison is required, while its three-day duration and manual approval are choices that leave the 48-hour bound uncertain.

alternatives.name: Fraud scoring as built
alternatives.summary: The solution computes recent card activity continuously, serves an XGBoost model synchronously with a rule fallback, and records score and model lineage for audits. A nightly retraining and shadow review workflow supports model updates, with a three-day review that leaves the 48-hour production target uncertain.

choices.reason: A transaction stream supports timely scoring inside the certified environment; a particular broker is not required.
choices.solution_quote: The payments switch publishes every card transaction to a Kafka topic inside the PCI-certified environment.

choices.value_id: Feature state: Flink aggregates in Redis
choices.reason: Recent activity must be available online and precomputed state supports the latency target. Flink and Redis are implementation choices, but maintaining online aggregates is strongly required.
choices.solution_quote: Flink jobs consume the topic and keep per-card aggregates (spend and counts over the last hour, day and week, and the number of distinct merchants) up to date in a Redis cluster.

choices.reason: The service needs a scoring model that can be retrained; the requirements do not select this model family.
choices.solution_quote: The model is a gradient-boosted tree model (XGBoost).

choices.value_id: Serving: Python REST container on Kubernetes
choices.reason: This is an in-environment deployable serving implementation. No requirement mandates Python, REST, or Kubernetes.
choices.solution_quote: It is packaged in a container with a small Python REST service and runs on the company's Kubernetes cluster, with six replicas and autoscaling on CPU.

choices.value_id: Capacity: Six replicas with CPU autoscaling
choices.reason: Replica scaling supports peak throughput, but neither six replicas nor CPU as the scaling signal is fixed by the stated target without measurements.
choices.solution_quote: with six replicas and autoscaling on CPU.

choices.value_id: Authorization behavior: Synchronous call with rule-engine fallback
choices.reason: A normal-path score must be available before authorization, and Q2 requires authorization to proceed when scoring fails. The existing rules provide the required fallback.
choices.solution_quote: The authorization switch calls the service synchronously with a 25 ms timeout. If the call times out or fails, the switch uses the existing rule engine for that transaction and logs that no score was used.

choices.value_id: Explanation: Return top three score-driving features
choices.reason: Feature explanations may help the dispute team, but R3 asks for the actual input values and model version, not a ranked feature explanation.
choices.solution_quote: The service returns, with every score, the three features that pushed the score up the most, which the dispute team uses to explain declines to cardholders.

choices.value_id: Score record: Append-only on-premises object-store table for 13 months
choices.reason: A durable per-score record of model and inputs retained for 13 months is required; an on-premises object store is one suitable implementation.
choices.solution_quote: Every score is written, with the model version and all input values, to an append-only table in the company's on-premises object store, kept for 13 months.

choices.value_id: Retraining: Nightly Airflow pipeline on last 90 days of labels
choices.reason: Regular retraining on arriving labels supports adaptation. Nightly cadence, 90-day window and Airflow are not uniquely specified by the requirements.
choices.solution_quote: An Airflow pipeline retrains the model every night on the last 90 days of labelled transactions.

choices.value_id: Experiment lineage: MLflow records parameters, metrics, training snapshot and artifact
choices.reason: Reproducible training provenance is needed to identify the data used for a model, but MLflow is a chosen implementation.
choices.solution_quote: MLflow records the parameters, the metrics, the training data snapshot and the model artifact of every run, and holds the model registry.

choices.value_id: Promotion: Three-day shadow comparison and manual risk-team promotion
choices.reason: Q4 requires comparison before production; this particular three-day duration and manual promotion are not forced and can conflict with the 48-hour bound.
choices.solution_quote: A new model first runs in shadow mode next to the production model for three days; the risk team reviews the comparison and promotes it by hand in MLflow.

choices.value_id: Operations visibility: Grafana drift and fallback dashboards and alerts
choices.reason: Monitoring score drift and fallback share helps operators detect problems, though these named dashboards are not explicit requirements.
choices.solution_quote: Grafana dashboards show the score distribution and the share of rule-engine fallbacks, and alert when the score distribution drifts from last month's.

adrs.title: Maintain recent activity for online scoring
adrs.context: The service needs a card's recent activity on the synchronous score path at peak transaction volume, while processing card data within the PCI environment.

options.name: Stream-maintained card aggregates
values: Ingestion: Kafka transaction topic
Feature state: Flink aggregates in Redis
pros: Makes recent per-card aggregates available without querying transaction history on each score.
Runs inside the company's certified environment.
cons: Requires operating a stream processor and a Redis cluster.
The exact p99 latency still needs measurement.
options.reason: R1 requires recent activity and Q1 favors having it ready on the online path. Maintaining aggregates is justified, although the named technologies are free implementation choices.

options.name: Query transaction history per score
values: Feature state: Query historical transaction tables for each score
pros: Avoids maintaining a separate aggregate state.
cons: Adds historical query work to every synchronous scoring request and weakens the peak latency case.
options.reason: This alternative can supply activity but does not support the latency requirement as well as maintained state.

adrs.title: Keep authorization available when scoring fails
adrs.context: Scoring is part of the authorization path, but a failure in the scorer or one of its data sources must not stop authorizations.

options.name: Bounded synchronous score with rule fallback
values: Authorization behavior: Synchronous call with rule-engine fallback
pros: Uses a score before authorization in the normal case.
Continues authorization using existing rules after timeout or failure.
cons: Fallback transactions receive weaker fraud detection.
options.reason: The normal score path and fallback behavior directly meet R1 and Q2; the 25 ms timeout is a chosen bound within the 30 ms target.

adrs.title: Retain enough evidence to reconstruct past scores
adrs.context: The team must answer audit questions about scores up to 13 months old, including the inputs, model version and training data, without sending card data outside the certified environment.

options.name: Retained score records and training lineage
values: Score record: Append-only on-premises object-store table for 13 months
Experiment lineage: MLflow records parameters, metrics, training snapshot and artifact
pros: Preserves each score's complete inputs and model version through the audit horizon.
Connects model artifacts to training data snapshots.
cons: Requires retention and lookup procedures across score and experiment records.
options.reason: These records provide the evidence R3 and Q3 require while keeping data in the company's environment. Specific storage and tracking products remain implementation choices.

options.name: Retain only latest score metadata
values: Score record: Keep only the latest score and model version
cons: Cannot reconstruct the inputs and model identity for an arbitrary older score.
options.reason: It misses R3 and Q3 because historical scores and input values are lost.

adrs.title: Retrain and compare models before promotion
adrs.context: New confirmed fraud labels arrive with delay, and updated models need comparison on recent transactions before production. The workflow must be practical for a small team and meet the 48-hour target.

options.name: Nightly retraining with shadow review
values: Retraining: Nightly Airflow pipeline on last 90 days of labels
Experiment lineage: MLflow records parameters, metrics, training snapshot and artifact
Promotion: Three-day shadow comparison and manual risk-team promotion
pros: Records the training run and compares a candidate with production before promotion.
cons: Three days of shadowing exceeds the stated 48-hour production window.
Manual review can add further delay.
options.reason: Retraining and comparison serve R2 and Q4, but the particular three-day review means this choice only partly meets Q4. The cadence, tooling and manual promotion are not forced.

options.name: Automatic promotion without comparison
values: Promotion: Promote every nightly model automatically without comparison
pros: Could shorten the time from training to production.
cons: Skips comparison with the current model on recent transactions.
options.reason: It misses Q4's explicit comparison requirement, even though it could promote faster.

adrs.title: Choose model serving and operating tools
adrs.context: The model must score inside the PCI environment at peak load and be maintainable by a small ML team using shared company infrastructure.

options.name: XGBoost service on Kubernetes
values: Model: XGBoost gradient-boosted trees
Serving: Python REST container on Kubernetes
Capacity: Six replicas with CPU autoscaling
pros: Packages model and service for deployment on existing company infrastructure.
Replicas and autoscaling provide a path to handle peak load.
cons: The stated replica count and CPU scaling require performance validation.
The requirements do not establish that XGBoost is better than another model family.
options.reason: This is a plausible implementation within the company environment. The model family, service language, orchestration and replica count are free choices; the latency target needs measurement.

adrs.title: Return score drivers and monitor operation
adrs.context: The dispute team explains declines, and operators need visibility into fallback use and changing score behavior.

options.name: Expose top features and monitor drift and fallbacks
values: Explanation: Return top three score-driving features
Operations visibility: Grafana drift and fallback dashboards and alerts
pros: Gives the dispute team a concise account of score drivers.
Makes changes in score distributions and fallback rates visible to operators.
cons: Top drivers do not replace retaining all inputs for audit reconstruction.
Thresholds and dashboard response procedures are unspecified.
options.reason: These choices support investigation and operations, but they are not forced by the listed requirements and do not substitute for the full audit record.
